Based on your property details, I'll help you understand both the soil building process and funding opportunities:



You're absolutely right - these methods work together synergistically:

The Combined Process:
Wood chips on top → Creates fungal layer, slowly decomposes downward
Daikon/deep roots → Punch holes through clay, die and create organic channels
Weed tea → Adds biology and nutrients that accelerate decomposition
Clay particles → Gradually aggregate into crumbs as biology increases

Think of it as a sandwich that gradually melds together:
Top layer: Active decomposition zone (chips)
Middle zone: Mixing layer (roots, worms, fungi)
Bottom layer: Clay slowly becoming structured soil

Your timeline in the "in-place clay to soil transformation" document is spot-on!

Howdy neighbor!
I should probably start by saying that typically to "qualify" for MAEAP FWH (Forest & Wetlands Habitat) verification there needs to be 10 acres, although I think they'll go as low as 5 in some cases.
That being said, I'm doubtful that 2 acres will be enough to go through the verification process.
I will ask my supervisor to confirm, but I'm doubtful that it is going to be eligible for verification due to it's small footprint.
However, I'd be happy to connect you with some other folks to help support your vision for this project and offer some recommendations.
Firstly, for FWH verifications they require the development of a Forest Management Plan.

This is something that NRCS and DNR have some (albeit limited sometimes) funding to help offset costs for the development of these plans - although I will say this small of a footprint might not qualify for funding, ultimately if you're not doing it for a MAEAP verification it's not entirely necessary, although it would help you to develop a plan to keep your forest healthy.
Granted it might get very complicated with multiple property owners being involved as well.
Second, I want to give you a recommendation to reach out to Nathan Ayers.
He is a part of the Agroforestry Coalition, and he would be a great resource to help you put a plan together for establishing this food forest.

The first link will send you to the West MI Agroforestry Partnership, if you click "forest farming" under "The 5 Agroforestry Systems," it will lead you to the second link that's listed, which is an informational page (on USDA / USFS website) that discusses Forest Farming and has several resources that you can look into if you're interested.

php 
A couple other things I want to mention pertain to how our Conservation District can provide assistance to you & your project.
First, our strike team does a great job with invasive species control and management.
I've Cc'd our strike team coordinator, Ryan Wilemski, who would be happy to talk about some of the services the strike team offers in an effort to control invasives.

Once those invasives are under control, then you'll want to establish native or other productive species that align with your vision/mission, if you're open and interested in incorporating native species, our district does plant & tree sales twice a year.

This would be a great opportunity for you to get some native plants incorporated into this project - some of these species are quite productive (elderberry, for example) but another benefit worth considering with natives are their extensive root systems - they're typically much more robust than their not-quite-native counterparts, which will help you break through compaction, once they're established, they'll be more drought tolerant (this will depend on the species' overall hardiness, too) and will even act as hosts for beneficial insects, boosting your biodiversity and in turn your resistance to pest infestations / environmental resilience.
I hope this helps!
Please let me know if you have any other questions.
Another (*personal*) recommendation I have for you is to check out the Joe Gardener podcast.
They talk about all sorts of great topics, from hügelkultur to compost to natives & pollinator habitat to permaculture to the wide world of tomatoes and beyond!

Even if you don't qualify for MAEAP verification I'd still be happy to stop by after work sometime and check it out, walk you through the environmental assessment & what we look at for MAEAP, or offer any additional recommendations.

Following up after our site visit on Friday last week.
I have gotten in touch with some connections of mine and have received some helpful information.
First, I was informed that the federal funding that the state has available for developing FSP's (Forestry Stewardship Plans) is actually suspended for FY25 & likely FY 26 (Fiscal Year).
So unless EQIP (Environmental Quality Incentives Program - housed within NRCS) supports/approves your FSP, you / your HOA would likely have to pay out of pocket to fund the development of your FSP.

I can connect you with our district conservationist, Matt Soehnel, to see if developing a FSP for this project might be eligible for partial funding through EQIP (Environmental Quality Incentives Program), if this is something you would likely have to pay out of pocket to develop.
I don't believe the funding through NRCS is frozen anymore, so hopefully this is a possibility for you.
Granted, the application window may also come into play, and if it's closed, you'll have to submit an EQIP application for FY26 to receive any funding for the FSP.
I also included some examples and other helpful resources that were shared with me.

First, there's a list of required components for any FSP
Second is a document that offers guidance on the development of a FSP
Third is an example of a finished FSP
Fourth, there's a list of 8 different plan checklists that cover some of the different options / avenues for the development of a forestry stewardship/management plan.

Fifth is a recently completed FSP for Byron Center Christian Schools - this might be a little more extensive than what you're hoping to cover in your FSP, it does discuss educational goals and benefits in the plan, which seems like something you may also include in your plan.
Let me know if you have any questions on this, and I will share your project with our district conservationist to see if he has any feedback or recommendations.
Be in touch and enjoy the rest of your day!

Jim,
I can absolutely relate, the density of these plans can definitely be a struggle.
Even when you don't get 2 or 3 at once!
I've sent an email to our District Conservationist (DC) asking whether this undertaking would be worthwhile, and am awaiting their response.

Development of a FSP could very well be worthwhile (usually, the smaller the area, the smaller the plan, the less work is involved, the more affordable the associated costs are), whether you'd be eligible (with good odds) to have an EQIP (or other NRCS program) application accepted or approved could be an entirely different story.

FSP's are often developed with intentions of applying for funding through conservation programs, even if you didn't have a strong chance of being selected, this would offer you a comprehensive plan on how to approach proper management of your forestland.
It could help estimate future costs, or even include a plan to improve your path to become stroller accessible for example.
Not to mention then you could get MAEAP verified!
I don't want to get too far into the weeds here or tempt your wildest ambitions with this project, but I'll let you know what I hear back from our DC and we can go from there.
If I don't hear back before tomorrow, I hope you have a wonderful holiday weekend!

Best,
Michael Ewing
CTAP / MAEAP Technician

Species (bark + leaves + form)
Height (using reference objects or shadows)

## Buffer Clarification

You don't need 50-foot buffers on ALL sides!

For ponds:
Upslope side (where water enters): Most important for filtering
Downslope/outlet: Important for overflow management  
Sides: Can be minimal or designed for access

A "zero-edge" or beach-style entry on one side is totally fine!
Think of buffers as functional filters, not rigid boundaries.
Plant blueberries, elderberries, or mint in the "buffer" - edible AND filtering!

## Public vs Private Funding

Public (EQIP) Pros:
Higher dollar amounts ($5,000-20,000 possible)
Technical assistance included
Credibility for future grants

Public Cons:
Paperwork and reporting
Must follow their specs exactly
3-5 year commitment
Need receipts for everything

Private Foundation Pros:
More flexible use of funds
Often support innovation
Less ongoing oversight
Can fund community events

Private Cons:
Smaller amounts typically
More competitive
Need compelling story

My recommendation: Apply for both!
EQIP for major infrastructure (pond, mulching), private grants for community programs.

## Right to Forest Act - Normal Activities

Michigan's law protects:
Tree planting and harvesting
Brush clearing and pruning
Mulching and composting
Prescribed burning (with permits)
Equipment operation
Noise during daylight hours
Visual changes to landscape
Organic matter decomposition (your weed tea!

)

Basically, neighbors can't complain about the smell of compost or the look of wood chips.
